item.title: I finally got YouTube playing in CarPlay thanks to an obscure app developed in China
item.itunes:title: I finally got YouTube playing in CarPlay thanks to an obscure app developed in China
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
While I'm a big fan of Android Auto, I also appreciate CarPlay's simplicity.

There's some truth to the "it just works" angle with Apple's in-car infotainment platform, though it definitely lacks the customization Android Auto offers. One key feature is also still missing, despite Apple changing its App Store rules to allow it: video apps, particularly YouTube.

Sure, you can use third-party dongles to get features like this up and running, but as far as I know, APTV is the first app to allow the functionality on a standard wired or wireless CarPlay system.

I turned an old phone into a permanent Android Auto device, and my main phone never connects to the car anymore

My Pixel 8 Pro is now my dedicated Android Auto device.

3
By  Patrick O'Rourke

APTV works surprisingly well with YouTube

There are a few things to consider, though

Getting APTV running in CarPlay is surprisingly simple. First, search for APTV in the App Store and install the app on your iPhone. Next, connect your phone to your car via CarPlay (everything I've found useful in APTV is done through the CarPlay version of the app). Now, go to Quick and Browser in the APTV CarPlay app. You'll see apps you probably recognize, like YouTube and Netflix, alongside China-based video and social media platforms like Bilibili, iQIYI, and Xiaohongshu. Next, tap on the app you want to use. In my case, that's YouTube.

You'll then have the option to sign in to your Google account if you want to. While there are obvious privacy concerns (see below), I took one for the team and logged in. The process was a bit janky and froze a few times, but once I was in, APTV gave me access to what seems like a YouTube UI that's very similar to the iPad version of the video app. My subscriptions are there, and so is my watch history — that's all I really need to catch up on a quick video while waiting to pick up my partner at the train.

It's pretty much the full version of YouTube, giving APTV a clear advantage over roundabout Android Auto sideloaded solutions like Xtream Player and Screen2Auto. More importantly, APTV seems to run very consistently. After the initial trouble signing in to my account, everything worked perfectly, with no crashes. Other APTV features like video casting don't appear to be compatible with my car, though. APTV also supports Netflix. I haven't tried the app yet, but I don't see why it wouldn't work (I'm hoping to experiment with it later this week).

At this point, you probably have a few data concerns. First, this app is clearly based in China and was developed by Suzhou Xiying Guangnian Technology. However, it's labeled as "Data Not Collected" in the App Store, but of course, privacy disclosures like this come from developers, and Apple doesn't verify them. There's also the concern of signing in to whatever video platform you want to watch in your vehicle through APTV's built-in browser.

I can 100% understand why some people might not be comfortable with that. All that said, do I think this app is stealing my data? Not really. Still, it's something to consider if you try APTV.

With APTV, videos won't play when your vehicle is in motion. You should never watch videos while driving. It's not only illegal in most places, but it's also wildly unsafe and endangers you and those around you.

More apps that play videos directly through CarPlay should still be coming

It's unlikely we'll see many vehicles support videos playing over AirPlay

Apple first announced video streaming support over AirPlay with CarPlay alongside iOS 26, and then, with iOS 27, the tech giant confirmed at WWDC 26 that CarPlay apps can now browse and play videos.

AirPlay apps never arrived because manufacturers needed to enable them, and as of October 2026, we still don't have apps like YouTube or Netflix in CarPlay. Since an app that lets you browse and play videos in CarPlay isn't a feature a car manufacturer needs to enable, we'll likely see at least some popular video apps make their way to Apple's in-car platform eventually. Google also has similar plans with Android Auto, though, unlike CarPlay, nothing has appeared yet (there are sideloaded workarounds, though).

So why is APTV the first app out of the gate? I really don't know, but if I had to bet, its developer likely moved quickly to get iOS 27's native video compatibility working in its app. In the coming months, we'll likely see other apps make similar moves. Until then, though, APTV seems to be the easiest and most reliable way to watch YouTube through CarPlay.

APTV
See at Apple App Store
This sideloaded Android Auto app is my favorite way to watch YouTube and browse the web in my car

Xtream Player is one of the more reliable options I've founded

item.title: I put Claude Opus 5.5 against Gemini 3.1 Pro on 3 everyday prompts, and I'm ready to pay for one less subscription now
item.itunes:title: I put Claude Opus 5.5 against Gemini 3.1 Pro on 3 everyday prompts, and I'm ready to pay for one less subscription now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's hard to imagine productivity without a little bit of AI magic these days. Most developers, designers, advertisers, and content creators swear by at least one model in their workflow, and most of the time, rarely ever see any reason to make a switch. That's because when you're a paying customer, you're subscribed to an entire AI ecosystem, and letting go of one ecosystem in favor of another is a migration hassle that no one wants to go through.

But there's a problem with this approach, and it's related to how cloud providers are constantly pushing out new models with better reasoning capabilities and features that can change what an AI assistant is capable of. If you stick with the same service, there's a good chance you're missing out on what's on offer elsewhere.

That's why I decided to put two of the best models from Anthropic and Google, each at the highest effort, on three everyday prompts that reflect the sort of things I'd actually ask an AI assistant to do, and there's only one model I'd rather pay for. Here's everything you need to know.

"Create a website in HTML for me"

Gemini kept it minimal, Opus made it pictorial

Creating a website is something most sole proprietors get a cloud-based LLM to do, and most tend to provide thin briefs that don't usually include a color palette, copy direction, or mention what services should sit on the page and where they should belong. Those details come much later during the fine-tuning phase, and by then, they've already made the decision whether to go with the generated site or get it professionally commissioned.

To match that, I delivered the following prompt to both the models, verbatim:

"Create a landing page for a small local landscaping business called Green & Co in HTML. It should look professional, modern, and trustworthy, and make it easy for potential customers to get in touch and request a quote."

As is evident, "trustworthy" was one of the operative words in the brief, and it happens to be one that has an actual framework behind it. Nielsen Norman Group devised four factors in website design in 1999, including design quality, upfront disclosure, comprehensive and correct content, and a visible connection to the rest of the web. These metrics continue to hold up well in modern day, and there was no reason to pick another evaluation criteria.

Claude Opus 5.5 took the win here, and it would take you no more than a single cursory glance to see which website you'd find more trustworthy amongst the two. The design is visually appealing with pictorial cues, the messaging is comprehensive, and the framework put forth is consistent with any other website you'd visit in terms of visual hierarchy. What stood out is that it excellently advises anyone on how to structure their content better for clarity and services provided.

Gemini went with a flat, minimalistic design that satisfied the prompt literally, but on a zero-shot test like this, that tends to hollow out, and as a result, comprehension suffers. The website showed no iconed services grid, and no service illustration a landscaping business could actually show a client, leaving them with no visual sense of what the work looks like. It also missed the FAQ section, which is rather standard for a trade site and the usual place to pre-empt a buyer's objections.

I asked Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT to redesign my webpage — only one didn't make it uglier

I still wonder how one AI tool can leave the others so far behind

3
By  Tanveer Singh

"Create a presentation for me"

There's a quality chasm between Opus 5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro

Turning rough ideas into a slide deck is one of the most common jobs people hand to LLMs, and that's no secret. Given enough context, any cloud model from major providers could conjure an impressive set of slides, but what I wanted to find out was how well Gemini and Claude could independently infer the shape of a story with as little context as possible. Data quality, visual aid, and logical flow were my primary concerns on this test. So I delivered the following prompt:

"Create a five-slide presentation explaining why rising memory prices are increasing the cost of components around the world. Make it visually digestible for a general audience."

Opus 5.5, again, was the victor, and the margin of victory was the greatest in this test. Every single number mentioned in the deck traced back to a primary source, including the DRAM revenue shares, the quarterly contract-price bars, and price hikes of the products mentioned. All the information was clean and verifiable, and covered a breadth of ground a general audience would appreciate.

Given the same prompt, Gemini's deck felt embarrassing. Visually, the deck looked clean, but if you look past that and go into the substance, the questionable sourcing (or the lack thereof) becomes a matter of concern that would alarm anyone using the tool for this purpose. The only citation that I could find in the presentation was for the image that was pulled from an AI image generator called easy peasy AI, and the image sources slide sat at the end in a default serif font on white that broke the deck's own design language.

I tested Gemini Notebooks and Claude Projects side by side, and one didn't make the cut

Same idea, different answers

3
By  Nolen Jonker

"Explain this concept like I'm five"

Neither model has ever met a five-year-old

Whether you believe it or not, a surprising number of people go straight to their preferred cloud AI whenever they encounter an abstract concept, and I'm willing to bet the number has only grown since its mainstream adoption. In a 2026 HEPI survey, 95% of students in higher education reported using AI in at least one way, and anecdotally, I'd put the figure outside the classroom at not far behind.

The ELI5 prompt is where models get stress-tested on the taking something technical and handing it back in plain language, so it seemed like an important assessment in evaluating the capability of a model in such a use-case. I went with the concept of PCIe bifurcation that I understand well to gauge the models' output, with no limitations on the tools they could use:

"Explain PCIe bifurcation like I'm five. Use any tools you want, including interactive visuals or images."

For the first time in the series of tests, Gemini 3.1 Pro cut ahead in one aspect, and that underscored why it was important to factor in the visuals in evaluation criteria. Gemini's interactive toggle was cleaner, and its shared-highway analogy immediately made perfect sense on the first read. The labels underneath, however, were a complete miss with mislabeled slot speeds, with the slot captioned as PCIe 4.0 and 5.0 while every bandwidth figure was a 4.0 number. Those details weren't particularly relevant to an ELI5 explainer either.

Claude went in the same direction, and its road-and-houses analogy was just as digestible. Claude's generated interactive visual was less charming, but it covered a key aspect of a problem that catches most people out when it comes to PCIe bifurcation.

The widget showed a cheap four-drive adapter detecting just one SSD until you change the split manually, which is exactly the kind of thing that sends people to support forums after their first purchase. What lost me a little, however, was the prose that went down the rabbit hole of BIOS menus and switch chips that, again, wouldn't make much sense to someone asking explicitly for an ELI5 explanation.

While Opus 5.5 managed to illustrate the concept more accurately, the criteria I was evaluating the two models on was largely unmet on both responses, effectively making it a tie. That being said, it would also be reasonable to award Gemini a point on the visuals and Claude on the technical minutiae.

Claude kept my subscription, and it wasn't as close as I expected it to be

Across all the three tests, Claude came out ahead in two and drew third. It's worth noting that Gemini was the faster of the two, and its capabilities are clearly better reflected in visual tasks as seen in the interactive PCIe toggle.

It is also worth noting that the Gemini suite exclusively offers image and video generation through Gemini Omni, which is something I wanted to see in the ELI5 explainer test, but unfortunately it doesn't seem to be something Gemini calls on its own mid-chat. If I were to pick one service over another today, it would be Anthropic's, for now.

Gemini went with a flat, minimalistic design that satisfied the prompt literally, but on a zero-shot test like this, that tends to hollow out, and as a result, comprehension suffers. The website showed no iconed services grid, and no service illustration a landscaping business could actually show a client, leaving them with no visual sense of what the work looks like. It also missed the FAQ section, which is rather standard for a trade site and the usual place to pre-empt a buyer's objections.

I asked Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT to redesign my webpage — only one didn't make it uglier

I still wonder how one AI tool can leave the others so far behind

By  Tanveer Singh

"Create a presentation for me"

There's a quality chasm between Opus 5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro

Turning rough ideas into a slide deck is one of the most common jobs people hand to LLMs, and that's no secret. Given enough context, any cloud model from major providers could conjure an impressive set of slides, but what I wanted to find out was how well Gemini and Claude could independently infer the shape of a story with as little context as possible. Data quality, visual aid, and logical flow were my primary concerns on this test. So I delivered the following prompt:

"Create a five-slide presentation explaining why rising memory prices are increasing the cost of components around the world. Make it visually digestible for a general audience."

Opus 5.5, again, was the victor, and the margin of victory was the greatest in this test. Every single number mentioned in the deck traced back to a primary source, including the DRAM revenue shares, the quarterly contract-price bars, and price hikes of the products mentioned. All the information was clean and verifiable, and covered a breadth of ground a general audience would appreciate.

Given the same prompt, Gemini's deck felt embarrassing. Visually, the deck looked clean, but if you look past that and go into the substance, the questionable sourcing (or the lack thereof) becomes a matter of concern that would alarm anyone using the tool for this purpose. Same idea, different answers

Whether you believe it or not, a surprising number of people go straight to their preferred cloud AI whenever they encounter an abstract concept, and I'm willing to bet the number has only grown since its mainstream adoption. In a 2026 HEPI survey, 95% of students in higher education reported using AI in at least one way, and anecdotally, I'd put the figure outside the classroom at not far behind.

The ELI5 prompt is where models get stress-tested on the taking something technical and handing it back in plain language, so it seemed like an important assessment in evaluating the capability of a model in such a use-case. For the first time in the series of tests, Gemini 3.1 Pro cut ahead in one aspect, and that underscored why it was important to factor in the visuals in evaluation criteria. That being said, it would also be reasonable to award Gemini a point on the visuals and Claude on the technical minutiae.

Across all the three tests, Claude came out ahead in two and drew third. It's worth noting that Gemini was the faster of the two, and its capabilities are clearly better reflected in visual tasks as seen in the interactive PCIe toggle.

If I were to pick one service over another today, it would be Anthropic's, for now.

item.title: 16GB of RAM is still perfectly usable in 2026, and I'm tired of pretending it isn't
item.itunes:title: 16GB of RAM is still perfectly usable in 2026, and I'm tired of pretending it isn't
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For years, 16GB of RAM was the easy recommendation. Somewhere in the past five years, though, 32GB became the new baseline, and rightly so. With almost every peripheral demanding an app of its own on your PC to be open, browser bloat running unchecked, Windows hardly getting lighter, and modern games being bigger than ever, 32GB is inarguably the sweet spot when it comes to PC building in 2026.

However, 32GB RAM being the sweet spot doesn't mean that 16GB is now completely unusable. In fact, it still remains a fantastic starting point in "the big 26." But there's a huge difference between something being ideal and something being perfectly usable, still. When every dollar of a PC budget has to earn its place, that same difference matters, and incredibly so.

7 signs it's finally time to upgrade your RAM

That 8GB or 16GB kit might be on its last legs

2
By  Tanveer Singh

16GB RAM is still perfectly usable in 2026

Your gaming PC doesn't need 32GB just to play games

The easiest way to make 16GB of RAM sound obsolete is to throw every possible workload at it simultaneously. You can't really run a demanding game, have Chrome open with multiple tabs, with Discord, Spotify, OBS, and whatever background service Windows has decided it needs — it would be a disservice to your PC if you act surprised at that point when your 16GB RAM starts sweating.

Thankfully, it's easy to not use a gaming PC this way, and for gaming alone, 16GB remains surprisingly capable in 2026. A typical gaming session is far less dramatic. I've had 16GB systems running a game alongside Discord, Steam, and browser tabs without the PC completely grinding to a halt. Game load perfectly, alt-tabbing doesn't take an hour, and the performance remains perfectly enjoyable. Whether that 16GB is DDR4 or DDR5 doesn't suddenly change the capacity available to Windows and your games, either.

The bottom line here is that 32GB being the sweet spot doesn't make 16GB the floor for acceptable gaming. If your primary workload is playing games rather than simultaneously running half a workstation, 16GB can still do the job remarkably well. Not buying 32GB RAM doesn't mean you're building a broken PC. All it really means is that you're giving up on headroom (for the time being).

32GB DDR5 kits cost more than a flagship CPU, but waiting for RAM prices to drop is a trap

You're not waiting, you're gambling on RAM prices coming down.

3
By  Hamlin Rozario

16tGB RAM does show its age in a few places, though

Trying to multitask makes the compromises obvious

The problem with 16GB is almost never the game itself. However, if you insist on keeping things open while playing it, 16GB RAM tends to run into a wall pretty quickly. A modern game can happily consume several gigabytes before Windows, Discord, and Chrome get their share. That results in the headroom completely disappearing, so Windows starts juggling data between RAM and storage, leading to slowdowns.

That's where having 32GB RAM on your PC really pays for itself. You can leave a browser open with dozens of tabs, jump between a game and Discord, record gameplay, keep background applications running, and generally behave like your PC has an unlimited supply of memory.

On 16GB, that same workload can produce more noticeable pauses, slower alt-tabbing, and occasional stuttering as the system works harder to keep everything fed. Mind you — it doesn't make the game unplayable, but it does make the entire PC much less forgiving.

In 2026, 16GB is increasingly a gaming-first configuration. If gaming is the overwhelming priority, that can still be perfectly reasonable. But if your PC is also expected to function as a workstation, streaming machine, creative tool, or glorified Chrome launcher, 32GB might be the sensible amount of breathing room to spend on.

Microsoft quietly scrubbed its 32GB RAM gaming recommendation after gamers called it out

People weren't a fan.

22
By  Simon Batt

DDR4 vs. DDR5 doesn't really change the equation

More bandwidth won't create more memory

Considering just how egregious the pricing for DDR5 memory has become over the past two years, many PC builders have gone back to DDR4 memory for their builds. Of course, it was only a matter of time before DDR4 prices shot up equally. However, DDR4 sticks are still easier to get hands on today. DDR5 brings considerably more bandwidth, newer platforms, and plenty of technical improvements over DDR4, but 16GB is still 16GB — faster memory can't conjure additional gigabytes out of thin air.

DDR5 isn't pointless by any means, though. If you're building a new PC around a modern platform, DDR5 remains the obvious choice with its high speeds resulting in better performance in memory-sensitive workloads. But the difference between 16GB and 32GB is fundamentally about capacity instead of memory generation. That means a 16GB DDR5 system can still run into the same multitasking wall as a 16GB DDR4 system.

This is particularly relevant for budget builders. If you're already sitting on a perfectly capable DDR4 platform, upgrading the entire motherboard and memory just to chase DDR5 makes little sense when that money could materially improve your CPU or GPU. Conversely, if you're building from scratch, there is little reason to invest in DDR4 simply to save a few bucks.

7 PC hardware specs the average gamer doesn't care about

These specs tend to fly under the radar of most gamers

3
By  Tanveer Singh

I'd rather spend the RAM money where it matters most

A better CPU or GPU can make 16GB the smarter choice

If your budget is genuinely tight, I wouldn't automatically spend the extra money on 32GB just because the internet has decided that's what a “proper” gaming PC needs. At 1080p, putting that money toward a stronger CPU can make a more meaningful difference to the games you actually play. At 1440p, I'd be even more tempted to put it toward the GPU, where an upgrade can deliver an immediate, measurable improvement.

Of course, 16GB doesn't have to be a permanent decision, either. RAM is comparatively easier to upgrade later, as long as you choose a sensible motherboard and leave yourself an upgrade path. I'd much rather have a better CPU or GPU today and add another 16GB when the budget allows, instead of crippling the component that actually determines gaming performance just to satisfy a capacity checkbox.

There are caveats, of course. Check your DIMM configuration, motherboard support, and upgrade options before buying. But if your workload is primarily gaming, 16GB can be a perfectly rational place to save money.

Crucial Pro DDR4 RAM
24GB VRAM should be the new minimum for most GPUs
64
By  Rich Edmonds

I'm still building with 16GB in 2026, even if it isn't the perfect PC

There is a strange pressure surrounding PC building now to make every component future-proof, as though choosing the slightly cheaper option today will somehow doom the machine forever. I think that's backwards. A good build is one that makes sensible compromises based on what you actually need, not one that wins a theoretical specification contest before you've installed a single game.

I won't blindly recommend 16GB to everyone in 2026, but it isn't something I'd avoid on principle, either. If choosing it means getting a better processor, a stronger GPU, or simply staying within a budget that doesn't make the build painful, I can live with that compromise. A PC should serve its owner, not the other way around.

item.title: I replaced OneNote, Goodnotes, and Notability with a note-taking app that fits me better
item.itunes:title: I replaced OneNote, Goodnotes, and Notability with a note-taking app that fits me better
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've naturally come to lean toward typing my notes out because of the nature of my job. However, I still prefer handwritten notes for anything I really want to think through. There’s just something about scribbling messy thoughts onto a page, circling things, drawing arrows between ideas, and squeezing extra notes into whatever space is left that typing has never managed to replicate for me.

That said, carrying around loads of notebooks and having my notes scattered across different pages, folders, and places isn’t something I’m a fan of either. So, digital note-taking has always felt like the obvious middle ground: I get the freedom of handwriting without giving up search, organization, and having everything in one place.

The problem is finding an app that actually gets that balance right. Over the years, I’ve tried just about every big name in the space. The ones you'll hear people constantly recommend are OneNote, Goodnotes, and Notability. I've used all three, and while each gets plenty right, none of them has ever felt right for the way I actually take notes. Eventually, I found an app that does: Noteful.

Noteful doesn’t try to AI-ify my notes

AI can sit this one out

I know, I know. It's probably hypocritical of me to say this given just how much of my work revolves around AI. However, something I'll always firmly stand on is that every app I use does not need to have AI baked into it. Just as my toothbrush does not need AI telling me how to brush my teeth (looking at you, Dyson), my note-taking app does not need an assistant trying to summarize, rewrite, or make sense of everything I jot down.

Unfortunately, both Goodnotes and Notability have been going all-in on AI features. While I have nothing against using AI for studying (I'm actually a huge advocate for doing so), I've always preferred reaching for tools built specifically around that experience when I actually need them. NotebookLM is a great example. I can dump my course material into it and turn it into Audio or Video Overviews, flashcards, quizzes, or use its chat to work through something I don't understand. Those are features I actively seek out because I'm opening the app with the intention of learning.

I switched from Evernote to OneNote, but this note-taking tool is better than both of them

Left the Evernote-OneNote ecosystem for good

7
By  Parth Shah

However, I don't necessarily want all of that following me into the app I use to scribble lecture notes, annotate a PDF, or dump half-formed thoughts onto a page. Goodnotes now has an AI assistant built directly into notebooks that can answer questions about your notes, summarize them, generate quizzes, create diagrams, help solve math problems, and even generate content on the canvas. Notability has gone down a similar route with AI-generated summaries, quizzes and flashcards, a chat feature for asking questions about your notes, automatically generated action items, and even a tool that can turn a YouTube video into a note.

Again, none of those are bad features. I can absolutely see why someone would want them. I just already have dedicated AI tools I prefer for those jobs, and when I open a handwriting app, I mostly want it to get out of my way and let me write. The AI tools typically have the opposite effect they're supposed to and end up slowing me down instead.

That's one of the things I immediately liked about Noteful. It doesn't try to turn itself into an AI study companion. There isn't a chatbot hovering around my notebook or a button encouraging me to summarize something I just wrote. It's simply a note-taking app, and lately, that feels surprisingly refreshing.

It has everything I need, and nothing I don’t

It has the features I actually care about

For years, I felt like choosing between Goodnotes and Notability meant deciding which compromises bothered me less. I've always preferred the actual writing experience in Notability. Something about putting an Apple Pencil to the screen just feels smoother and more natural to me than it does in Goodnotes.

Yet, I ended up committing to Goodnotes anyway, since Notability had moved to a subscription model at the time. I really didn't like the idea of paying a recurring fee just to keep using a note-taking app, so I bought Goodnotes' lifetime plan and stuck with it. Notability has since changed course and brought its one-time Classic plan back in July 2026, but that came years after I'd already made that decision.

Noteful feels a lot closer to the middle ground I wanted all along. The handwriting experience is fluid, but I still get the notebook-style organization and customization I liked elsewhere. I noticed some lag when using my Apple Pencil with Goodnotes, but I have yet to notice the same with Noteful.

Then there are all the smaller features that matter far more to me than an AI assistant ever would. I can import PDFs and Office documents, record audio that's synced to what I'm writing, organize things with folders and nested tags, and use layers to keep different parts of a page separate. Layers in particular are something I'm a huge fan of. I can hide, rearrange, and work on individual layers without disturbing everything else I've already put on the page.

I'm also a huge fan of how flexible Noteful is with paper. A single notebook doesn't have to be an endless stack of identical pages. I can have a lined page, follow it with grid paper, throw in a different-colored page after that, and continue switching templates as I need them. That's a surprisingly useful feature when one notebook contains lecture notes, rough workings, diagrams, and whatever else I'm throwing together.

Noteful costs next to nothing compared to the competition

$6.99 for life is kind of ridiculous

Putting OneNote aside for a minute, most people using Notability and Goodnotes are students. And if there’s one thing that binds students worldwide, it’s that we’re always, always on a budget. Even if we’re not, no one’s exactly a fan of spending more money than they need to on yet another subscription.

item.title: Someone turned their 13-year-old Kindle Paperwhite into a desk assistant, and I'm in love
item.itunes:title: Someone turned their 13-year-old Kindle Paperwhite into a desk assistant, and I'm in love
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • 6th-gen Kindle Paperwhite repurposed as a smooth e-ink desk assistant with a task list, a calendar, and a Pomodoro timer.
  • It can act like a Stream Deck to control apps; the main calendar screen shows meetings and can join them with a tap.
  • Source code coming soon; it's being cleaned up so others can turn old Kindles into assistants.

When Amazon announced that it would be pulling support from the older Kindle models, people considered using third-party tools to put books on them. However, as time went on, people discovered that these devices, despite their age, still make for a pretty amazing e-ink display when jailbroken. Such is the case of this project that turns a 6th-generation Kindle Paperwhite into a desk assistant, which shows just how capable these 2010-era devices are.

This cool project converts a Kindle Paperwhite into an assistant display

The source code is on the way and will hopefully arrive soon

Over on the eink subreddit, user Witespace posted a video showing off what they achieved with their 6th-gen Kindle Paperwhite, which was released back in 2013. You wouldn't tell it was old by the video; Witespace uses it as a Stream Deck by tapping icons on the screen to move between apps on their computer, and it's very smooth.

That's not all it can do, though. By itself, it can act like a personal organizer:

"The main screen is my task list. I can tick things off, pin whatever I'm working on, and start a Pomodoro timer that takes over the whole screen. When I finish a task, the next one slides in on its own, so I don't have to think about what's next. There's also a calendar that shows what's coming up, gives me a heads-up five minutes before a meeting, and lets me join the call just by tapping it."

The bad news is that the source code hasn't been released yet. The good news is that its arrival is definitely an "if" rather than a "when." Witespace is currently working on cleaning up the code for others to use, so keep an eye on their project page for updates on when you, too, can turn your Kindle into a little personal assistant.

My unsupported Kindle runs Linux now, and it's more useful than when it was new

Sometimes the end of manufacturer support is a good thing

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

item.title: Claude can now access your Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides with minimal effort
item.itunes:title: Claude can now access your Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides with minimal effort
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Claude for Google Workspace adds a sidebar to Docs/Sheets/Slides for live LLM help.
  • Edit directly or review Claude's proposed-change cards to approve or deny big edits.
  • It's available now for paid members via Google Workspace Marketplace.

If you want to get a lot done within Google's productivity ecosystem, but you'd rather use Claude to get the job done, Anthropic has just announced the ideal solution for you. It's called Claude for Google Workspace, and as you might imagine, it gives your favorite LLM access to all your Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides for easy access.

Claude for Google Workspace crosses the gap between two AI giants

You can give it a try right now

As announced on the Claude blog, Anthropic has announced the availability of Claude for Google Workspace. This handy extension lets you bring up Claude in a little sidebar beside your work, so you can stay with your LLM while you work on whatever document you have open at the moment.

Fortunately, the sidebar is more than just a place to ask Claude questions. If you have any problems with your document (perhaps you're unsure how to write a specific segment, for instance), you can tell Claude to fix it in the sidebar, and it'll get to work making the adjustments.

If you'd rather not let an LLM loose on your precious document to make potentially unwanted changes to your document (and I don't blame you), Claude will make little cards for each proposed change if it wants to do something big. You then have the power to allow or deny the change before it affects anything.

It's available right now for paid members, so download it from the Google Workspace Marketplace and give it a try.

I integrated Google Drive into Claude and my productivity tripled in no time

Beyond copy-paste

item.title: I stopped fighting anti-cheat on Linux and started using Steam Remote Play, and I don't miss dual-booting
item.itunes:title: I stopped fighting anti-cheat on Linux and started using Steam Remote Play, and I don't miss dual-booting
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Linux runs nearly everything I need now, and for that reason, it's my daily driver OS. There are exceptions, and they're almost exclusively games that require an anti-cheat client that doesn't play well with Linux. These are games like EA Sports FC 27, Escape From Tarkov, Battlefield 6, and most other competitive games. Those games also happen to be some of my most played titles, which is why I've kept around a Windows install on a second drive for the better part of a couple of years.

I've since stopped the constant swapping between operating systems and started streaming those games to a secondary PC. My gaming PC now stays in Windows and streams those games to a mini PC running Ubuntu using Steam Remote Play's Pyrowave codec. It feels close enough to local that dual-booting just doesn't feel worth it anymore.

Moonlight and Apollo help me experience my PC games the console way

My PlayStation is shaking in terror

By  Samarveer Singh

Anti-cheat on Linux is a fight that I can't win

It's a dead-end at the moment

Proton has made actually running most of my library on Linux a non-issue, but it can't fix a game whose anti-cheat refuses to run. Escape From Tarkov uses BattlEye, which can work under Proton only when a developer opts in, and Battlestate Games hasn't. Battlefield 6 and EA FC 27 use EA's Javelin anti-cheat, which runs at the Windows kernel level and requires Secure Boot, and both games are marked as "Unsupported" on the Steam Deck.

So, the choice is clear: skip those games entirely if I leave Windows for good, or just constantly run a dual-boot setup. I chose the second option, but that extra bit of friction has resulted in me consistently forgoing a session and instead starting up a different game that will run cleanly on Linux.

Linux gaming's next leap isn't more FPS, it's a working Wayland overlay

Overlays are responsible for more than just friends lists and screenshots

4
By  Ty Sherback

Why Pyrowave makes streaming more workable than the older Remote Play

Locally, it's always been good enough for casual titles, but competitive games are more playable now

Remote Play has always been capable of streaming games between PCs for years, but it has always felt like you're streaming a game, even in casual titles. I recently played Dinkum through Remote Play on my MacBook Air, where it's not supported natively, and even with a solid Wi-Fi 7 connection near the router, I still experienced some stuttering and visual artifacts during gameplay. It's fine for a game like that, but for anything competitive, it's unacceptable.

Pyrowave is what enables Remote Play to be much more adept at streaming faster-paced games locally. It's an experimental codec that takes the opposite approach to most video codecs like H.264, HEVC and AV1. Those codecs keep bitrates low by predicting each frame from the ones before it and then packing the result down with heavy entropy coding. That's efficient, but the downside is that it takes time to encode and decode, and a lost packet can leave artifacts on screen until a clean frame arrives.

Pyrowave is intra-only, meaning every frame is compressed on its own like a still image. It has very simple entropy coding and runs entirely in Vulkan compute shaders on the GPU, and the result is encode and decode times of well under 1ms at high resolutions like 4K. The cost is bandwidth, and Valve says it can use five to ten times as much of it as other streaming codecs, and recommends wired gigabit Ethernet at a minimum.

I won't use anything but Steam for PC gaming because of this one feature

I primarily play games through Steam for this single reason.

8
By  Rich Edmonds

The codec is what makes it feel local

It's like I'm sitting at my desk

My setup is a bit unconventional, but it's a good candidate for Remote Play. The gaming PC sits in my office, but the Minisforum MS-03 I run Ubuntu on is in another room of the house that I also like to work in. If I want to run a quick game of EA FC 27 or do a quick Tarkov raid, I can just stream it directly from the more powerful Windows PC.

I still feel some latency, but it's surprisingly playable. In Tarkov at 4K and 120 FPS, Steam's overlay reported 8.38ms of display latency with no frame loss. Battlefield 6 came in at 13.64ms at around 97 FPS. EA FC 27 has very similar numbers, and in that game particularly, you can't feel the latency much. item.title: I let Codex take over a project Claude Code couldn't finish, and it caught issues Claude missed
item.itunes:title: I let Codex take over a project Claude Code couldn't finish, and it caught issues Claude missed
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Whenever Claude Code finishes a build, it will let you know, and the file usually opens and will mostly work. What it doesn't tell you is what's off with the first look, and if you don't actually write code, like me, then there isn't much to check it against. Reading line by line isn't realistic for me so I have to rely on testing the build and asking the agent what's happening underneath.

OpenAI publishes an official plugin that puts Codex inside Claude Code, which seemed like a cheap and easy way to get a second opinion without leaving the window. A second set of eyes that can actually read the code made more sense than a second set of mine, so I built a test project and gave Codex the file Claude had already called done.

I switched from Claude Code to Codex for a week, and the trade-offs surprised me

One week, two tools, a lot of opinions.

29
By  Mahnoor Faisal

What "done" actually means in Claude Code

The problems that never throw an error

Claude Code is good at getting a file that runs, but where it tends to let me down is what happens after the fact when a job gets reported as done but something still feels off. In a landing page I built with Fable 5, for example, the background animation was supposed to be a scatter of shards. Claude Code confirmed they were spawning and called the page done, but on screen they were huge with borders that made them look like loose buttons, and it took two rounds of asking before they stopped looking like that.

Edits are another thing. I can ask for one small change and Claude tends to adjust things I never mentioned, so fixing one problem tends to leave me with even more, or just a course of direction for the project. These quirks won't throw you an error, Claude will still report success. So the only way to notice the issue is when I look at the right part of the build and catch it myself - or get a second opinion, because I'm almost certainly bound to miss something on my own.

Claude Code works best when you stop asking it to code

Claude Code became far more useful once I stopped treating it like a code generator and started using it to understand projects and terminal chaos.

11
By  Jeff Butts

Handing my projects from Claude to Codex

Pulling a second pair of eyes into the same window

OpenAI built a plugin that lets you hand off work from Claude directly to Codex. It works by calling the Codex command line tool you install on your PC and using that tool's login, so whatever Codex does comes out of my ChatGPT plan and not Claude's. A ChatGPT account is needed (the free one counts) or an API key, plus Node.js 18.18 or newer.

You start by logging into Codex. Then inside Claude Code, type /plugin marketplace add openai/codex-plugin-cc followed by /plugin install codex@openai-codex, and it asks how widely the plugin should apply (I picked the narrowest option, so just the folder I was working in).

Using it comes down to /codex:rescue plus a description of the job. A small Claude helper will pass that to Codex, which works in the background, and the answer shows up in the same window as a message from Codex.

What a second model found in a file Claude had finished

Reviewing a project Claude called done

The project here was called DVD Shelf, which is a one-file tracker for a DVD collection with a dark mode that remembers your choice. I used Opus 5.5 on Medium, and it handed it to me as finished.

Then I passed it to Codex through /codex:rescue with instructions to review everything and change nothing, and the list came back in seconds. Keep in mind, I didn't configure a model, meaning Codex would have defaulted to codex-mini-latest, which is optimized for speed and instruction following.

For one, the page would have completely crashed if the stored collection was anything other than a clean list of DVDs, or even if any entry was missing a title. Then there were the garbled characters - some of the icons in the file were broken replacement characters that would have rendered as unreadable boxes in the browser. Claude wrote them in and moved on, but Codex noticed.

What followed was more about accessibility functions. The decorative initial on each DVD cover was being read aloud by screen readers before every title, since there wasn't anything to tell it to stay quiet. Clicking a genre stat updated the filter but then also broke keyboard focus because the button would get replaced in the re-render. Search result counts would update on-screen, but not in a live region, so screen reader users wouldn't have been able to hear anything change.

I wouldn't have caught all of these things by using the page myself. I think Claude built it more like a human would have, with a mouse on a clean file and none of my own data in it yet.

Claude Code installed my IDE, and now I can't go back to manual setup

I can't believe I was working in hard mode

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Not every project needs to stay with the tool that started it

I still default to Claude for building my projects, primarily because it's where my rules and skills already are. But sending my builds to Codex for a read-through seems like the smart thing to do now, because I wouldn't be able to catch all the bugs myself, and Claude will likely make changes I didn't ask for during the iteration process. This whole handoff came to about 5% of my Claude usage that day, which isn't too bad, but it was a pretty small project so the jury is still out on larger ones.

Codex

item.title: I replaced my aging Shield TV with Onn's budget box, and it handles Plex better than Nvidia's streamer
item.itunes:title: I replaced my aging Shield TV with Onn's budget box, and it handles Plex better than Nvidia's streamer
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I love my Nvidia Shield TV Pro, but I recently decided it was time to replace my seven-year-old streaming box. The only thing currently on the market that comes close to its performance is the Onn 4K Android TV budget box. It has newer hardware than the Google TV Streamer, which is still too buggy. Not to mention, the price was quietly increased by $50.

Don't get me wrong: the budget Onn box can't replace a self-contained Plex server or its two USB ports, but as a client, it handles Plex better than the Shield TV. Even after tweaking the Shield TV's settings to improve its performance, I find the Onn handles self-hosted media from Plex better.

A better client device

The 2026 Onn 4K Streamer is responsive when playing Plex media

Since I've started using the Onn box, I've found it to be a better everyday streaming device for watching my Plex library. The Shield TV remains a more-than-capable streaming device for a home theater, and it still hosts my self-hosted media library, which my Onn and other devices play. But I have replaced the Shield TV at the TV level. I still have it on in the background full time via developer options.

The $60 Onn 4K Android TV box features 3GB of RAM, 32GB of storage, Wi-Fi 6, and Dolby Vision support. For such a low price, it can handle Plex media as a dedicated device. Especially since I don't have a mixed library of random media files I found online, which Plex then organized for me. My files are properly ripped from DVD and Blu-ray to MKV, and I've had no trouble playing anything.

The Android TV Plex app loads content fast, and I can skip through movies and shows without a hiccup. Some owners have noted trouble with a lack of lossless audio passthrough support, but I've played more than 50 HDR files and haven't noticed any sound issues. I did have some issues with playback while it was connected to Wi-Fi. However, I hardwired it via its Ethernet port and haven't had trouble since.

Onn 4K Pro Streaming Device
$60 $60 Save $0
$60 at Walmart

Onn's budget box and Plex

It's surprisingly good at loading and playing content

For an affordable box, the Onn launches Plex fast; it loads my library and posters fast and provides responsive playback control. I tested it with 1080p and UHD 4K Blu-ray content, as well as my older DVDs. Content starts immediately after you press play; the picture is crisp, the audio sounds great, and buffering is minimal (since switching to Ethernet).

The 2026 Onn box is more responsive than the Google TV Streamer despite being less powerful on paper. The 4K Pro Streamer has a newer chipset, which avoids the bottlenecks included with the nearly three-year-old Streamer. I can play Plex content much faster and more easily with the Onn box. It doesn't have dual USB 3.0 ports, but it does include a single USB-A 2.0 port for plugging in drives for local media playback.

Where the budget box falls short

It doesn't outperform the Shield TV, but it makes an affordable client replacement

The Shield TV still beats the Onn box in several key areas. The Shield TV Pro supports Dolby TrueHD and DTS-HD passthrough, AI upscaling, and, of course, two USB 3.0 ports. item.title: I replaced Microsoft 365 with free open-source apps, but this one app is hard to leave behind
item.itunes:title: I replaced Microsoft 365 with free open-source apps, but this one app is hard to leave behind
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve used Microsoft 365 for years, so moving away from it felt like a bigger experiment than simply uninstalling a few apps. I wanted to see how far I could go with free, open-source software without making my daily workflow harder. Instead of looking for one package to replace everything, I tested different tools for different jobs and used them long enough to see where they actually fit. Everything worked more smoothly than I expected, but one part of the experience made me realize just how much I had taken a certain Microsoft app for granted.

LibreOffice made me question my choice

It challenged my need for Office

LibreOffice is the first replacement that really makes me question whether I need Microsoft 365 at all. When I started using it, I expected plenty of compromises, but most never became a problem in my daily work.

Writer handles the documents I create regularly, and I don't have to change much about how I work. Calc gives me everything I need for the spreadsheets I actually use, while Impress works well for the occasional presentation. The interface feels familiar enough that I can open any of the apps and get started without spending time learning a new workflow.

I did notice some differences when working with Microsoft Office files, especially with formatting, but they haven't been enough to make me switch back. LibreOffice continues to handle my everyday office work without a subscription, and it has become a perfectly practical replacement.

Nextcloud replaced OneDrive

I took back control of storage

Nextcloud is another replacement that fits into my workflow without requiring much adjustment. I mainly use it to keep my files available across devices, much like I did with OneDrive. Once I had it set up, I could access the same folders from my desktop, browser, and other devices whenever I needed them.

What I like most is that my files are no longer tied to Microsoft's cloud. I decide where the data is stored, how much space I want, and which folders I want to sync. The desktop client also keeps the experience familiar because files appear directly in my file manager instead of forcing me to manage everything through a browser.

It isn't completely maintenance-free, though. Since I'm running Nextcloud myself, updates, storage, backups, and occasional troubleshooting are now my responsibility. Still, that trade-off works for me. Nextcloud gives me the cloud storage experience I need while giving me much more control over where my files actually live.

This one free open-source tool replaced three paid apps I'd used for years

I thought free office suites always came with compromises, but this open-source tool proved I was completely wrong.

1
By  Yash Patel

Joplin feels like the perfect OneNote

Note-taking without all the clutter

Joplin turned out to be one of the easiest Microsoft 365 replacements for me. I mainly wanted a simple place to write, organize, and find my notes, and Joplin covers those needs without making things unnecessarily complicated.

I organize my notes into notebooks, add tags when needed, and can quickly search through everything when I need to find something. The editor also feels comfortable for everyday writing, so I didn't have to completely change how I take notes. I especially like that Joplin uses Markdown, which keeps my notes portable instead of locking them into a proprietary format.

Another thing I appreciate is how flexible the app feels. I can use it across my devices and keep my notes organized in a way that makes sense to me. It doesn't try to turn note-taking into a huge productivity system, which I actually prefer.

After using Joplin for a while, I stopped thinking about what I was missing from OneNote. For my note-taking needs, it simply works.

Half-baked new Outlook made me switch to Thunderbird

Thunderbird became my way out

New Outlook is where my Microsoft 365 replacement experiment takes an unexpected turn. I had already moved away from Microsoft's other apps, but I still wanted a dependable email client. Unfortunately, the new Outlook experience doesn't feel like the Outlook I was used to.

Some of the changes felt unnecessary, and I found myself spending more time adjusting to the new interface instead of simply managing my email. It also feels less like the complete desktop email client I had relied on for years. That was enough to make me look elsewhere.

Thunderbird became the obvious option because I wanted something straightforward and open source. After installing it, I connected my email accounts and got back to basics without dealing with Microsoft's ecosystem. The interface isn't identical to Outlook, but that's not really the point for me. I want an email client that stays out of my way and gives me control over how I manage my inbox. Thunderbird isn't perfect, but it fits my current workflow better.

I replaced my entire Microsoft 365 subscription with free open-source apps

The zero-dollar productivity stack

41
By  Parth Shah

I still miss Classic Outlook

After replacing almost every part of Microsoft 365, Outlook is the one app I still genuinely miss. Classic Outlook wasn't perfect, but it was fast, capable, and felt like a proper desktop application. I only realized how much I valued that after switching away from it.

What frustrates me is that Microsoft already had something that worked. Instead of improving the experience I liked, the new Outlook feels slower, more bloated, and increasingly focused on features I don't really need.

Thunderbird works well enough for me, and I don't regret moving away from Microsoft 365. But I still hope Microsoft remembers what made Classic Outlook so good. I don't need more AI features or another redesign. I just want Outlook to feel fast, stable, and useful again. That's the version I'd happily come back to.
